You have attempted this same task before and did not succeed. These are the plans you wrote after those attempts.
Trial #1: New plan: I failed because I attempted to calculate a conditional probability $P(kwox | jyka)$ by dividing by zero ($0/0$), which is mathematically undefined, and then incorrectly tried to force a "Yes" or "No" answer based on an incomplete causal intuition. The core mistake was ignoring the strict mathematical definition of conditional probability when the conditioning event has zero probability. In causal inference, if $P(jyka) = 0$, the counterfactual $P(kwox | do(jyka))$ or the observational $P(kwox | jyka)$ is undefined, making the comparison "smaller" logically invalid. I should have immediately recognized that the question asks for a comparison between a defined value ($11\%$) and an undefined value, concluding that the statement cannot be true or false, or that the premise of the comparison is impossible. My new strategy is to first check if the conditioning event has non-zero probability. If $P(jyka) = 0$, I will explicitly state that the conditional probability is undefined and therefore the comparison cannot be made, rather than attempting to derive a numerical value or guessing a boolean answer. I will structure my final answer to clearly identify the division by zero error as the reason the "chance" cannot be determined to be smaller.
